people.summary: Selected uncertain identity: the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455 and Stirling witness of 1475–1480 are modelled as one man. Both source groups remain separate and intact. A compatible 33-year adult career and shared civic role favour this provisional model; father–son and other-family alternatives remain open. Birth and death unknown. His two selected uncertain father links remain conditional, with no additional parent or component-join credit.

identity_selection.basis: Select the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455 and the Stirling witness of 1475–1479/80 as the same man, at low confidence. Both groups use compatible John de Glasgu/Glasgw name forms in burgh-property witnessing, and the August 1475 catalogue places the Stirling John among burgesses. An adult active in 1447 could still witness in 1480 in his fifties or older. The conventional circa-1450 Stirling birth was inferred from an assumed young adult in 1475; it cannot establish a second man. A single compatible civic career is the simpler working model than inserting another generation from that estimate.
identity_selection.limitations: No shared holding, relative, trade, personal seal or distinctive repeated associate joins the cities. people.name: George Glasgow of Mureistoun
people.summary: Prefer the named George of Mureistoun as James Glasgow-991’s probable father. George is recorded at Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder obligation; the accepted 1605 original-register reading places James’s household in probable Muirestoun and names an adult George Glasgow as witness to the baptism of James’s son George. The earlier review already assessed the two adult George occurrences as probably one man. The same uncommon surname, the probable same holding across nineteen years, and the older name-bearer’s personal participation in the younger household favour lineal family continuity. Father is the preferred degree: an older established man followed by James’s child-bearing household is a normal two-generation sequence, and the child’s George name is compatible with that reconstruction. This is a combined locality/household inference, not three independent proofs or a compulsory naming rule. The 1605 witness’s residence and age are unstated, and Muirestoun remains a probable reading/location. Shared holding names do not prove a legal title transfer. Father, uncle, older brother, cousin and neighbour remain genuine alternatives. The 1586 obligation does not establish muster attendance, and neither record states that George was James’s father. The George name and witness role are supporting context, not direct kinship. Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains an unselected uncertain father alternative; his 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel, not James. The George comparison supplies a closer holding-and-witness association than the broader Andrew/Calder model, without proving that Andrew could not be James’s father. For the working tree only, select William Glasgow-3522 as George of Mureistoun’s uncertain father through the surviving possible identification with the Glasgow merchant George Glasgow-1099. Protocol 2903 explicitly names that merchant’s deceased father William; protocol 2916 gives his mother and curator. The same rare full name and compatible 1586 generation make the merchant an existing-profile comparison for the Mureistoun man. The father proof belongs to the merchant: transferring it to the Mureistoun account depends entirely on the unproved identity. This is a testable named upstream route, not direct evidence of a Calder-to-Glasgow movement or a newly proved son of William. The merchant was a minor in 1586, with the accepted approximate birth range 1565–1572. If James’s conventional circa-1575 birth were established, that would conflict with his being the merchant’s son. James’s birth is unrecorded: a later birth in the 1580s can fit the 1605 fatherhood and, toward the earlier end of George’s range, ordinary fatherhood in the previous generation. Those are compatibility examples, not new birth estimates. The 1598 marriage-contract comparison does not prove a first marriage or identify James’s mother. No date is altered to make this route fit. George-1099 stays a compatible candidate; there is no merge, no second distinct George son claimed for William, and no automatic transfer of Margaret Herbesoun or a wife as mother. If the two Georges are different men, William’s upstream placement must be reconsidered. The retained George Glascoe-36 and George-3171 comparisons remain open on their actual source limits. 20 October 2026: Edward-1557 is now a selected uncertain son at 26%, choosing a brother route alongside James-991; the former Corsankell father remains an 18% alternative. No mother or upstream identity is changed.

people.name: John Glasgow, Prescott watchmaker
people.summary: John Glasgow, Prescott watchmaker with wife Jane in deed B13, is selected as Robert Glasgow-4150’s brother at 98% subjective confidence. Robert’s 1849 will gives brother John one sixth. John and Jane’s 1856 deed transfers an undivided one sixth of the same Dibble Street lots to Samuel, who is another will-named brother. The exact locality, buyer, parcels and fraction identify the grantor strongly; B13 does not itself expressly call John Robert’s brother. John’s birth, death and parents are not named, and his identity with an existing John profile is unresolved. Extend the existing Alexander Glasgow-3904 father hypothesis to John and Mary at 27%, uncertain, conditional on their documented membership in the Prescott sibling family. Thomas-987 and Daniel-3896 already carry this father, and Samuel-4010 and Robert-4150 already have the same selected uncertain hypothesis. Its basis remains the single late descendant tradition naming Alexander as Thomas’s father, with compatible generation and sibling inference. The original will and deeds name no parent. These two extensions supply no independent parent testimony and do not raise the existing estimate; no mother is selected. These are two previously unstructured record accounts recovered from evidence already researched in September, not two newly discovered sources or two proven additional distinct people. John retains six unselected compatible or weak existing-profile comparisons; later residence, spouse or death elsewhere is not by itself an exclusion of a possible migrant. No Mary Black/Glasgow match is established in the bounded local historical catalogue check. Both accounts remain on identity hold before any new WikiTree profile creation. Record dates are not birth dates.

people.name: Janet Broun
people.summary: The Findmypast transcript records Samuel Glasgow and Janet Broun, both resident in Dalziel, in banns dated 23 June 1716: OPR 639/1, item 2, p.71. It gives marriage year 1716 but no separate ceremony date, ages, occupations or parents. The transcript was inspected on 18 October 2026; the original register was not inspected. Prefer the 1716 Dalziel groom as Samuel Glasgow-3166, the father named in James’s 1719 Dalziel baptism index. The same full name, exact parish and three-year interval make one household more likely than two contemporaneous Samuel Glasgows. The selected working couple is assessed as probable at 88% subjective confidence, including the groom-to-profile identity. This rates the proposed couple identified by banns, not proof of a completed wedding. The record-defined intended couple is explicit; the link to the later father is inferred, without a residence below parish level or a named parent. Janet is a possible maternal lead for James Glasgow-3523, not his assigned mother: banns alone neither prove a completed marriage nor establish the mother of a later child. Samuel’s own parents remain unknown. The existing James-to-John Glasgow-3094 working father proposal remains possible at 41%; the new banns do not bridge the seventy-year identity gap. All birth/death fields, mothers and existing father grades are preserved. No new paternal component is joined and no certainty upgrade is counted.

people.name: John Glascow / Glasco, Trinity student
people.summary: Select Thomas Glasco-144 as the Trinity student John’s probable working father at 63% subjective confidence. The original college entry names father Thomas, described as Artifex (craftsman), and says John was born in Dublin. The preferred existing account is the Dublin Thomas already tentatively identified with the watchmaker active in 1773–1783. The uncommon full name, same city, appropriate adult generation and actual craft occupation together make that account a better fit than name and age alone. A further family clue is the 1784 Dublin baptism of John, son of Thomas Glasco and Eliza Hynes: the 1779 watchmaker’s marriage names Miss Hynes. The directory independently supplies Thomas’s forename and the exact Ormond Quay address of the watchmaker; the bracketed Thomas in the marriage extraction is editorial, not another independent name statement. Prefer the 1784 St Michan’s baptism and the 1800 Trinity student as one John at 72% subjective confidence. Both name John Glasco/Glascow, father Thomas and Dublin; the college age of 16 on 10 June 1800 puts a literal birth window at 11 June 1783–10 June 1784, compatible with a later 17 September 1784 baptism but not a recorded birthday. The Hynes marriage/baptism correspondence and the father’s craft description give the proposed family more specificity than a date-and-name match. The Catholic baptism and scholarship in 1803 leave a material religious-history gap: contemporary accounts describe exclusion of Catholics from scholarships. A baptismal affiliation need not remain unchanged throughout life, but no conversion or mixed-marriage history has been found or inferred. Another John or another Thomas remains possible. Select the record-defined Eliza Hynes as John’s probable mother at 72%, conditional on the preferred baptism-to-student identity. The baptism transcript expressly names her as mother of its John; the college page names no mother. Her identification with the watchmaker’s 1779 Miss Hynes is a further probable comparison, not a recorded marriage for this named Eliza. No marriage to Thomas Glasco-144 is installed, and the Duffy, Catherine and Mary King households retain their own identities and grades. The 63% father estimate assesses the whole link to the modern Thomas-144 account, including its unresolved watchmaker identification; it is lower than confidence that the printed student had a father named Thomas. Thomas-173’s 1760 Sarah/Catherine household, Thomas-143 and an unrepresented namesake remain alternatives. Thomas-173 has no independently recorded trade in the reviewed baptism. The baptism is a Findmypast transcript, not an inspected original; North Anne Street is the church/parish description, not a proved family address. These subjective percentages are not measured frequencies or independent values to multiply. John’s later identity remains on HOLD: John Glasgow-3946, diedThurles 1871 aged 87, and John Glasgow-3751 of the 1820 Abbeville census remain compatible comparisons. No identity merge, live WikiTree edit, exact birth date, father replacement or new connection between existing profile components is claimed.

people.name: Lillias Stewart
people.summary: The Barony banns transcript names Samuel Glasgow and Lillias Stewart on 24 February 1790, OPR 622/7, item 1, p 42, register 1778–1819. It gives marriage year 1790 but no separate wedding date, ages, parents, occupation or residence field. The transcript was inspected on 21 October 2026; the original register was not inspected. Select the record-defined Lillias Stewart as the probable mother of James Glasgow-1483 at 86% subjective confidence. The 1790 Govan baptism explicitly names Samuel Glasgow and Lilias Stewart; the independently recorded Barony banns name that same distinctive full parent pair shortly before either disputed baptism date. This supports one local household across the two registers. James’s adult account has a Govan nailer burial in 1833, aged 42, and children Samuel and Lillias with Jean Cunningham. Parish, approximate age and the paired family names favour identification with the 1790 child. The granddaughter’s Lillias name is supporting naming evidence, not proof. The 86% assesses the complete maternity proposition for the adult James, including the child-to-adult identity. It is not the near-certain named maternal role for the indexed 1790 child alone. The baptism dates 22 March and 25 April remain unresolved versions of one underlying event; no original was inspected. The banns identify neither man as a nailer. James’s burial age suggests about 1790–1791 and is not an exact match to the indexed child. A different James or Samuel remains possible. No birth, death, parents or childhood identity is assigned to Lillias from the contributed 1766 estimate.

chronology.reason: James Glasgow-2682, father of the Edinburgh Duffe household, probably represents the same adult as James Glasgow-1150, the weaver apprenticed on 16 June 1641 and admitted burgess on 20 June 1649: 70% subjective identity confidence. The 1696 James and 1699 youngest-son Thomas apprenticeships name a father James Glasgow, weaver and burgess of Edinburgh. Thomas’s maintained 1684 baptismal identification and the Duffe household’s James children of 1679 and 1680 fit those apprenticeship ages and the youngest-son order. The older craftsman independently has that specific craft and civic status, with an exact master/date cross-reference between his 1641 apprenticeship and 1649 admission. The maintained admission review found one matching admission, although this does not establish uniqueness. His marriages to Bessie Whyte on 6 July 1649 and Agnes Duncan on 11 November 1653, followed by Agnes’s burial as the weaver’s wife on 21 January 1674, permit a later Duffe household beginning in 1677. Successive marriages explain the wife sequence without requiring another same-name weaver and burgess. The circa-1655 birth, previously inferred from the first known child in 1677, is a creation estimate rather than an age or birth record. The preferred older-adult identity independently supports birth before 16 June 1641, uncertain and conditional on that identity. Replace the local preferred estimate with that boundary, retaining the old circa-1655 and “by about 1657” reasoning as superseded history. This is a separate vital/identity correction, not a date altered solely to fit Robert’s 1647 burial. No exact birth year is established; retain the broad Midlothian birthplace without claiming a new birthplace record.
